newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentine mutual fund assets seen at $3.5 bln.
newsitem.headline: Argentine mutual fund assets seen at $3.5 bln.

text.p: Argentina's mutual funds will manage some $3.5 billion at the end of this year, an increase of nearly 50 percent, a top official said.

"Judging from projections we have made, the total value of assets under management at the end of the year will be around $3.5 billion," Oscar Falleroni, president of the chamber that oversees the institutions, told Reuters.
The steep rise in the assets managed by the funds is due to the massive influx of savings by investors who have discovered a new way of investing their money.

Argentina's first mutual fund was established in 1960, but growth in the sector was unspectacular in the following 30 years as Argentina's economy was dogged by hyper-inflation and low domestic savings rates. There were 29 funds in 1990.

The expansion has taken off in the 1990s due the stability to Argentina's economy brought about by the introduction of "Convertibility" - the pegging of the value of peso to the dollar at par since 1991. That has stimulated increased savings.
"The growth has been explosive. The public is starting to understand that the variety of investments by the funds allows for efficient administration of their savings," said Falleroni.

The funds on offer are also giving investors more choices. Falleroni estimated that at the end of 1997 there will be between 220 and 250 different funds compared with 160 now and 110 a year ago, when $918 million of funds were under management.
In the last two months alone, 12 new funds have been set up, of which five are run by Banca Nazionale del Lavoro.

One of the reasons Argentine mutual funds' popularity is spreading is the high returns they give. During 1996, variable-rate funds had returns of up to 39 percent, while investors in fixed-income funds received an average return of nine percent.

Falleroni said one of the benefits is the fact that investors can chose between funds that invest in instruments with low volatility compared with those that are exposed to every market movement such as stock funds.
Although Argentine funds offer investments in a wide array of bonds, stocks and other instruments, nearly 80 percent of the $2.34 billion under management is placed in fixed-income instruments.
